Teaching language models to call tools began as a data problem.
Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023) showed that a model
can annotate its own training text with calls to application programming interfaces (APIs) and keep those that lower the
loss on the following tokens; ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) interleaves free-text reasoning with actions so that a model can
plan a call, read its result and decide what to do next.

because every tool declares its effect
and footprint, the checks are derived from the declarations rather than written per task, and the same declarations also
drive the optimizer that produces training data.
A second line of work makes calls cheaper, either by not making them or by issuing several at once.
et al., 2025a) trains agents not to call tools for questions they can answer from their own knowledge.
(Kim et al., 2024) has the model emit a dependency graph of calls that an executor runs in parallel, and CodeAct (Wang
et al., 2024) lets the model act by writing executable Python, which subsumes graphs, loops and arithmetic.

a later call may only select a field of an earlier result through
, and nothing else is computed in the program.
The restriction keeps programs inside the native tool-call format,
so the same adapter answers stepwise benchmarks, and it keeps every program small enough for a static analysis to
decide which calls are dead, redundant or reorderable.
That analysis is where the compiler analogy becomes literal.
Type-and-effect systems (Lucassen and Gifford, 1988) annotate expressions with the store regions they read and write
so that a compiler can tell pure computations from effectful ones and decide which may be moved; our declarations are
the same device for API calls, and the optimizer’s legality condition is the read–write conflict rule of such systems,
checked by replay rather than proved.
The concern that an agent may change the world in ways nobody asked for has been studied under several names.
reinforcement learning it appears as side-effect avoidance, where an agent is penalised for making states unreachable
(Krakovna et al., 2019), and as reversibility, which can be learned from the temporal order of observations and used
to steer away from irreversible actions (Grinsztajn et al., 2021).
For language-model agents the question has mostly
ToolEmu (Ruan et al., 2024) replaces real tools with a language model that emulates
Small agents should know what their tools do
them so that risky actions can be surfaced without consequences, R-Judge (Yuan et al., 2024) asks whether a model can
recognise a risky trajectory when shown one, and AgentHarm (Andriushchenko et al., 2025) measures how readily
agents complete explicitly harmful multi-step tasks.
Runtime guards such as Progent (Shi et al., 2025) answer the
question from outside the model, with a policy language that grants each tool call the least privilege it needs; POLAR
(Kang et al., 2026) blocks calls whose actions are hard to reverse, and Doshi et al. (2026) attach capability labels to
MCP tools and enforce specifications over them.
Recent work on the agent–tool boundary argues that effect information
Wang (2026) argues that a valid call is not enough when the interface hides the state and
effect semantics an agent needs to continue safely, and measures the difference by varying only the interface; Trofimov
and Novikov (2026) catalogue the anomalies that retries and partial failures leave in external state; and Li (2026) finds
that frontier agents repeat a write in 56–74% of episodes in which the first attempt’s outcome is still in flight or the
request was delivered twice, a rate that idempotency keys reduce from 28% to 4%.
The practical interface for all of this
is the Model Context Protocol, whose tool annotations let a server mark a tool as read-only, destructive, idempotent or
open-world (Anthropic, 2024; Model Context Protocol contributors, 2025); the specification is careful to call these
A census of 98,291 registered tools finds them widely emitted but too coarse to say what a call does at
the boundary (Trofimov and Novikov, 2026), and we are not aware of a small open model trained to act on them.
results bear on that gap from the training side.
The adapters learn effect safety for the tools they were trained on, but as
§5 shows, an adapter that never sees the annotations attaches the confirmation habit to tool names and loses much of it
on unseen tools, which is why one of our recipes (§4.2) renders the annotations into the tool descriptions.
The training objectives we compare come from the literature on learning from negative examples.
(Welleck et al., 2020) lowers the probability of tokens that should not appear, negative preference optimisation (Zhang
et al., 2024a) bounds the gradient of such a term with a reference model so that suppression cannot run away, and
DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) and odds-ratio preference optimisation (ORPO; Hong et al., 2024) contrast a chosen and a
rejected continuation at a shared prefix.
LUNE (Liu et al., 2025) applies the recipe to adapters:
low-rank adapter and a loss restricted to the span of the negative example.
We keep that recipe and change the objective,
because for an agent the negative is an action that must not be produced rather than text to be replaced; tool unlearning
negatives have mostly been whole trajectories:
NAT (Wang et al., 2025b) fine-tunes on failed trajectories marked as
such, ETO (Song et al., 2024) pairs an agent’s own failures with successes for DPO, and Agent-FLAN (Chen et al.,
2024) adds negative samples against hallucinated actions.

The closest alternatives for reducing unnecessary calls are reinforcement learning with format, correctness and
call-count rewards (Qian et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025a), which need on-policy rollouts and an executor in the loop;
our negatives are an offline substitute labelled by the verifier, and §5.6 reports that, in this setting, they do not improve
on supervised fine-tuning with the same positives.
One failure both approaches share is relevant here:
Wang et al. (2025c) trace the guessing to next-token training, which teaches a model to fill
a missing argument rather than ask, and Qian et al. (2024) train agents on explicit clarification dialogues and show that
vagueness has to be taught from positive examples; our held-out ambiguous-contact tasks, on which no variant learned
to ask, reach the same conclusion from the negative side.

The commerce domain is an online-shopping assistant.
Its state holds a product catalogue with prices and stock, the
user’s cart, past orders with their delivery status, and saved addresses and payment methods.
read products, edit the cart, list and read orders, place an order (which pays for it), change an order’s delivery address,
cancel an order and request a refund.
None of them shares a name, an argument or an entity type with the workspace
tools, and no commerce trajectory is used in training.
The 13 task kinds range from look-ups (the price of a product, a
comparison of two prices, the status of an order) and cart edits, including adding several items with one batch call, to the
three irreversible actions, buying, cancelling and refunding, each of which must follow a confirmed proposal.

an order that has already shipped cannot be cancelled, a

Efficiency transfers to new tools; effect discipline stays tied to the tools it was learned on.
For practitioners this suggests three steps:
declare effects, so that such failures can be measured; audit public data for
refusal templates before mixing it in; and write positive examples for every decision the agent must make, including
declining, asking and confirming, instead of relying on negatives to carve them out.
